entry.title: refactor(enrichment): fill the reading in order from one shared reque…
entry.content:
refactor(enrichment): fill the reading in order from one shared request pool

Preparation was three schedulers that happened to share a claim. Translation and
grammar each ran waves of three and waited for their own slowest request, and
audio did not start until both text layers had finished the entire reading — so
on a sixty-sentence story the last sentence's English arrived before the first
sentence's clip.

`PreparationPacer` is a leaf service that knows about order and pressure and
nothing about aids. Every request any layer wants to make asks it for a permit,
and permits go to the lowest waiting (sentence position, layer). That one
comparator is the whole front-to-back rule; the three stores keep everything they
already own well and gain no dependency on each other.

`PREPARATION_CONCURRENCY = 10` replaces the three per-layer ceilings, so how fast
a reading fills no longer depends on which layers happen to be outstanding. There
is still no client-side rate limit: the only reaction to load is a back-off
driven by a real 429's own Retry-After, which holds new grants without abandoning
what is already in flight.

Translation still runs its first batch alone to settle the reading's English
names; after that the glossary is a ledger read at permit time and written on
completion. Grammar loses its wave loop, audio loses its priority queue and fixed
worker array, and the lane starts every eligible layer at once.

Stopping a long reading now costs more in-flight requests than it did, because
more were running. Every one of them is still stored.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(enrichment): stop text preparation failing for reasons Monosai ca…
entry.content:
fix(enrichment): stop text preparation failing for reasons Monosai caused

Four independent causes, none of them a rate limit.

The enrichment JSON Schemas sent `minItems`/`maxItems`, which strict Structured
Outputs rejects; the 400 mentions `response_format`, so every batch spent its one
format recovery on a second full-price request, forever. The counts now live in
the array descriptions, where they were always only guidance — the real
constraint is enforced in `domain/ai` and `domain/enrichment`.

A refused native schema is now remembered through a `StructuredOutputMemo` port
and persisted with the text-model settings, so the discovery is paid once per
model rather than once per batch.

`finish_reason: 'length'` was parsed and never read, so a reply that ran out of
room surfaced as a malformed answer and spent a recovery a different request
shape could not help. It is now `context-budget-exceeded` with the issue code
`reply-truncated`, with its own copy and no recovery. Reply budgets are sized
from the batch, translation and grammar review default to minimal reasoning, and
enrichment finally uses the 60 s deadline that was defined for it and referenced
nowhere.

One bad id no longer destroys ten sentences: `partitionTranslations` keeps what
came back and the run re-asks once for the rest. An id that was never sent still
voids the reply.

The compatibility probe now sends the shape production sends — an array of
objects with a nullable field — so a recorded `native-schema` verdict is one the
model can keep.

Also fixes the translation lane reading `settings()` instead of
`configForTask('translation')`, which made a configured preset request a
different model than the reader's popover and write cache keys neither could
read back.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(reader): stop the opening press selecting the sentence sheet
entry.content:
fix(reader): stop the opening press selecting the sentence sheet

A held line raises the sentence sheet while the finger is still down, and the
sheet arrives under that finger. The platform then finished the very same press
as a text selection over the sheet's own Japanese, so asking to read a sentence
also handed back a selection nobody asked for — one press carrying two meanings
again, one step past where ADR 0058 left it.

On touch the sheet now starts inert and arms itself when that press ends, which
leaves selecting its text a deliberate second hold. A mouse is untouched: it
selects by dragging, which was already a separate gesture. The rule is named on
the sheet and repeated on its source, because a descendant that opts into
selectable text stays selectable under an ancestor that is not.

The end-to-end check holds a line and reads the rule that decides a selection
rather than asking Chromium for one, since synthetic pointer events cannot
produce a native selection; longPress is split into hold and release so a test
can look at the surface mid-gesture.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: test(reader): run the mobile-only reader checks on mobile alone
entry.content:
test(reader): run the mobile-only reader checks on mobile alone

Both checks assert behavior that only exists on a phone, but the desktop project
runs every journey, so each failed there rather than on the device it describes.
The drag handle is rendered only for a docked sheet, and the bar reaches the
viewport edge before any scrolling only because a phone pulls the reader into
the shell's top padding; a desktop keeps that padding and pins the bar on scroll,
which the test already asserts separately.

Both now use the isMobile fixture the rest of the file uses to tell the two
devices apart, rather than comparing viewport widths against the breakpoint.

entry.title: feat(reader): open a word by tapping and its sentence by holding the …
entry.content:
feat(reader): open a word by tapping and its sentence by holding the line

The double tap carried two meanings resolved after the fact, and the scroll that
kept a sheet clear of the tapped word cancelled the gesture that same tap had
begun. A tap is now answered by whatever it landed on, and a 450ms press opens
sentence details while the finger is still down. Repeats on touch are inert;
mouse and keyboard behaviour is unchanged.

The reading surface gives up native selection and the platform callout under a
finger only, because that press is now the application's gesture. Details are
quieter with it: an icon route to the sentence, grammar always readable, sheets
capped at half the viewport with the handle and action tray always reachable,
and anchored cards closing from their own corner. See ADR 0057.

entry.title: fix(vocabulary): align the standing line and stop it contradicting th…
entry.content:
fix(vocabulary): align the standing line and stop it contradicting the list

The count and its detail are two type sizes on one line, and the flex row that
holds them never set a baseline, so the smaller half rode high against the bold
number.

With no sources at all the same line read "0 words · from an unrecorded source"
while the row underneath said there were none. Removing the last source leaves
an empty snapshot behind, which is the standing of a fresh install; it says so.
A snapshot that still has words keeps its count whatever the list shows.

entry.title: feat(vocabulary): one Anki entry, a list, and a page per source
entry.content:
feat(vocabulary): one Anki entry, a list, and a page per source

The Words section asked a question the learner could not answer — "Anki" or
"AnkiDroid bridge", when the device decides which can work — and asked for the
AnkiConnect port before anything had failed. Every setting a source has lived in
its list row, so four sources were four stacked control panels and no list.

The platform is now a port, decided once at the shell edge, so one Anki entry
picks its own adapter and its own copy; iOS says plainly that a file is its only
route. A row carries the name, where the words came from and how many, and opens
a page where the settings are ordered by how often each is touched. Failures are
told in the sheet the learner pressed Anki in, each with the one link that
unblocks it and its code beside the doc keyed by those codes. The port moved
there, behind a fold, next to the retry it changes.

No stored data changes shape.
